bibliographic.title: Human-in-the-Loop Models for Ethical AI Grading: Combining AI Speed with Human Ethical Oversight
bibliographic.citation_apa: Selvam, M., & González Vallejo, R. (2025). Human-in-the-Loop Models for Ethical AI Grading: Combining AI Speed with Human Ethical Oversight. EthAIca, 4, 413. https://doi.org/10.56294/ai2025413

methodology.method_family: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) framework design with university case study/pilot evaluation
methodology.study_design: Four-layer HITL grading framework applied in a mid-sized university pilot on undergraduate essays
methodology.sample_description: 800 undergraduate essays at a mid-sized university; pilot used fine-tuned RoBERTa on anonymized faculty-scored essays
methodology.technology_context: AI-assisted educational grading using transformer-based language models (GPT-4, BERT, RoBERTa), rubric-aligned automated scoring, SHAP/LIME explainability, on-premise deployment with access control and privacy measures

eligibility.decision_rationale: Strong fit for LLM governance, human oversight, audit trails, explainability, and high-stakes educational assessment, but no conversational, chatbot, agent, or RAG system context; relevant as supporting evidence for HITL governance patterns rather than central conversational-governance evidence.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Abstract refers to 'the chapter' while metadata lists a journal article; confirm publication type and whether full methods/results beyond abstract-level claims are reported.

appraisal.notes: Provides a structured four-layer HITL framework and reports pilot outcomes (87% validation, 13% overrides, 40% time reduction), but supplied text offers limited detail on evaluation design, statistical analysis, and generalizability beyond one institutional pilot.

cerqual.explanation: Claims are internally coherent and supported by reported pilot metrics, but evidence is largely descriptive, institution-specific, and not focused on conversational LLM systems; adequacy is moderate for governance themes and lower for conversational-governance relevance.

coding.theme: Human-in-the-loop governance for LLM-based educational assessment
coding.subtheme: Ethical oversight and auditability in high-stakes grading
model_layers: pre-grading configuration with customizable rubrics and model calibration
preliminary scoring using transformer-based language models
human validation and contextual adjustment of AI outputs
transparent feedback supported by dual-logged audit trails

synthesis.main_claim: A four-layer Human-in-the-Loop grading framework can combine transformer-based LLM speed with human ethical oversight, transparency tools, and audit trails to improve fairness, efficiency, and trust in high-stakes academic assessment.
synthesis.contribution: Proposes an operational HITL architecture for ethical AI grading and reports a university pilot where faculty validated most AI scores, overrode a minority for contextual reasons, reduced grading time, and improved satisfaction through transparent educator involvement.
synthesis.limitations: Supplied text does not detail full study methods, validation metrics, or independent evaluation; findings come from a single institutional pilot; no conversational-system governance evidence; abstract wording suggests possible chapter origin requiring bibliographic verification.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence on HITL governance, human override/review, audit logging, explainability, and regulated educational deployment of LLMs; not suitable as central evidence for conversational governance.

evidence.claim: Article presents a four-layer HITL grading framework integrating AI recommendations with human oversight.
evidence.excerpt: the chapter presented a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) grading framework that integrated AI-generated recommendations with human oversight. The model consisted of four layers

evidence.claim: Framework includes transformer-based language models and human validation with audit trails.
evidence.excerpt: (ii) preliminary scoring using transformer- based language models; (iii) human validation and contextual adjustment of AI outputs; and (iv) transparent feedback supported by dual-logged audit trails

evidence.claim: Empirical pilot involved 800 undergraduate essays at a mid-sized university.
evidence.excerpt: A case study was conducted at a mid-sized university, where the framework was applied to 800 undergraduate essays

evidence.claim: Pilot outcomes report high human validation rate, override rate, and time reduction.
evidence.excerpt: the faculty validated 87 % of the AI-generated scores with only minor adjustments, while 13 % required overrides

evidence.claim: Context involves high-stakes educational assessment and ethical risks.
evidence.excerpt: ethical challenges, including algorithmic bias, contextual insensitivity, and reduced transparency, particularly in high-stakes assessments

evidence.claim: Specific LLMs named for rubric-aligned scoring include GPT-4 and BERT.
evidence.excerpt: transformer-based language models such as GPT-4 or BERT. These latter models pose significant risks of opacity

evidence.excerpt: selection of appropriate large language models (LLMs), incorporation of interpretability mechanisms, and configuration of a modular system architecture

evidence.claim: Pilot deployment used fine-tuned RoBERTa with privacy and access controls.
evidence.excerpt: integrated a fine-tuned version of the RoBERTa language model hosted on an on-premise server configured with institutional access control and data privacy measures

evidence.claim: Explainability tools SHAP and LIME are used to build trust.
evidence.excerpt: built trust through explainable AI tools such as SHAP and LIME
